paragraphs: Poisoning attacks damage a learned model by changing its training data, for example by inserting carefully chosen examples. Many such attacks assume the attacker knows the clean training set. This paper asks whether an attacker without that access could achieve equally damaging results, even if they know the distribution from which the training data comes.

The authors study this question theoretically for feature selection with LASSO. They compare an attacker who tailors poisoned examples to the actual training set with the strongest possible attacker who knows the data distribution but cannot inspect that set. They prove a separation: access to the particular training examples can make the attacker substantially more damaging.

The result makes the attacker's information a central part of the security question. In the studied setting, knowing the population distribution does not substitute for knowing the realized training set. Consequently, attack capabilities and defense results cannot simply be transferred between these two information settings. The demonstrated separation concerns LASSO feature selection, rather than establishing the same conclusion for every learning algorithm.
neurips-2021-a-separation-result-between.tldr: For LASSO feature selection, attackers who see the training set can provably cause much more damage than optimal attackers who know only its distribution.

paragraphs: A regression model can describe uncertainty by predicting quantiles: values associated with different positions in the possible outcome distribution. If those predictions match the true conditional quantiles at every level for each input, they provide an accurate representation of uncertainty. This paper examines how to move toward that goal beyond the commonly used pinball loss.

The authors argue that optimizing pinball loss can restrict which regression models are usable and make it difficult to target particular uncertainty properties. Their proposed methods support any class of regression model and allow an explicit balance between calibration and sharpness. This gives users a way to weigh whether intervals have appropriate coverage against how narrowly they describe possible outcomes.

The methods also target calibration for centered intervals and aim to produce more accurate conditional quantiles. The paper evaluates them experimentally, including on a high dimensional nuclear fusion uncertainty task. Its contribution is a broader set of tools for shaping uncertainty predictions around the properties that matter, rather than relying on one loss to deliver all of those properties together.
neurips-2021-beyond-pinball-loss-quantil.tldr: New quantile methods broaden model compatibility and let practitioners explicitly target calibration, sharpness, and centered prediction intervals.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to allocate a single indivisible object when nobody initially knows whether its quality is good or bad. Each potential recipient has a noisy but informative private signal. Motivated by discarded donated organs, the authors consider a social planner who wants to learn the object's quality while dealing with recipients who act strategically.

Under sequential offering, strategic behavior can lead to herding, which interferes with learning from recipients' information. The resulting decisions may allocate the object incorrectly and reduce welfare. The authors propose incentive-compatible mechanisms built around a dynamic voting process: agents participate in batches, and majority decisions guide the process. Truthful information elicitation is therefore part of the allocation design.

The paper proves that these voting mechanisms improve the probability of a correct allocation when agents are sufficiently well informed. It also shows that a simple greedy algorithm can achieve an improvement and uses simulations to quantify the gains. The information condition matters: the result supports the proposed mechanism under that condition, rather than claiming that majority voting always improves allocation.
neurips-2021-counterbalancing-learning-a.tldr: Batch voting mechanisms can improve allocation decisions over sequential offers when strategic agents have sufficiently informative private signals.

paragraphs: Many attempts to understand deep learning summarize a dataset or a model with a few aggregate measurements. This paper instead studies individual examples and asks how difficult each one is for a network to predict. It introduces effective prediction depth as a measure of the computational difficulty associated with making a prediction for a particular input.

The investigation finds relationships between an example's prediction depth and the model's uncertainty, confidence, accuracy, and speed of learning on that example. The authors also divide difficult examples into three interpretable groups and show that deep models process those groups differently. They demonstrate that using this understanding can improve prediction accuracy.

This perspective connects several observations that had previously been reported separately. These include earlier layers generalizing while later layers memorize, earlier layers converging sooner, and networks learning easy examples and simple functions first. The contribution is an example-level account linking internal computation with learning behavior. The reported relationships come from the authors' investigation; they are not presented as universal laws governing every network or input.
neurips-2021-deep-learning-through-the-l.tldr: Effective prediction depth links individual example difficulty to network behavior and helps explain several patterns in deep learning.

paragraphs: Differentiable programs combine program structure with parameters that can be trained through differentiation. Their structure can support interpretation and composition, but finding a suitable architecture requires searching a rapidly growing collection of discrete possibilities. This paper addresses the cost of that search, which earlier approaches largely handled through enumeration aided by pruning heuristics.

The authors represent architecture search as learning a probability distribution over program derivations generated by a context-free grammar. They then relax the discrete choices among grammar rules into a continuous search space and apply gradient descent. Learning which derivations are unlikely allows the method to prune them, directing search toward more promising program architectures.

Experiments on four sequence classification tasks show that the resulting synthesizer finds architectures whose differentiable programs achieve higher F1 scores while using search more efficiently than the compared state-of-the-art synthesis methods. The central contribution is to make the architecture choices themselves amenable to continuous optimization. The reported results demonstrate the value of this formulation on the evaluated tasks, alongside the interpretability and compositional motivation for using programs.
neurips-2021-differentiable-synthesis-of.tldr: A grammar-based continuous search method finds differentiable program architectures more efficiently and with higher F1 scores on four sequence classification tasks.

paragraphs: Active learning chooses which unlabeled examples should receive labels so that a classifier can learn effectively. This paper studies that choice for text classification. It starts from Expected Loss Reduction, which uses a Bayesian estimate of how much a label would reduce classification error, and changes the objective used to judge a candidate example.

The proposed BEMPS framework estimates improvements in strictly proper scores, including log probability and negative mean square error. The authors prove convergence results using techniques associated with Mean Objective Cost of Uncertainty. They also introduce a batch selection algorithm that encourages diversity in the expected score changes across unlabeled data, so selection considers differences in anticipated learning effects.

For experiments with pretrained language models, the approach combines ensembles with dynamically constructed validation sets. The evaluation compares acquisition functions within this broader setup. BEMPS using mean square error and log probability consistently outperforms the other functions tested. These findings support selecting examples through expected improvements in probabilistic scores, with batch diversity providing a complementary way to organize the labeling decisions.
neurips-2021-diversity-enhanced-active-l.tldr: BEMPS selects text examples by expected improvements in proper probabilistic scores and outperforms the other acquisition functions tested.

paragraphs: Neural networks can perform well on data resembling their training examples while struggling with related distributions they have not seen. This paper explores an architecture motivated by the idea that reusing and composing knowledge may help with such generalization. Neural Interpreters organize computation inside a self-attention network into modules called functions.

The model learns end to end how to route inputs through sequences of these functions. Computation can be composed across both width and depth, giving the architecture flexibility in how modules are combined. The design also supports extending model capacity after training. The emphasis is on learning a reusable organization of computation alongside the functions that perform it.

The authors evaluate image classification and visual abstract reasoning using Raven Progressive Matrices. For classification, Neural Interpreters match a vision transformer with fewer parameters and transfer to a new task efficiently in terms of examples. For abstract reasoning, they are competitive with state-of-the-art approaches on systematic generalization. These results support the architecture across two settings without establishing that modular routing resolves distribution shift in general.
neurips-2021-dynamic-inference-with-neur.tldr: Neural Interpreters learn to route inputs through reusable functions, showing efficient image classification and competitive systematic visual reasoning.

paragraphs: Video action recognition requires learning both visual appearance and changes over time. Its memory and computation costs often force training with small batches, making representation learning challenging. This paper introduces Dynamic Normalization and Relay, or DNR, to improve normalization in that setting by using relationships within video clips and across network layers.

The authors observe that existing networks commonly share normalization parameters across videos and overlook dependencies between neighboring frames and neighboring layers. DNR adds two lightweight recurrent modules to use those dependencies. Their parameter estimates depend on current features and on normalization information from nearby frames at the same layer or from preceding layers across the clip.

The authors first insert DNR into established two-dimensional convolutional backbones and evaluate on Kinetics and Something-Something. They report top-1 accuracy improvements exceeding 4.4 percentage points over baselines without additional training embellishments. Further experiments with three-dimensional backbones and other spatial-temporal networks support its effectiveness. The results indicate that adapting normalization using temporal and layer context can materially improve the tested action recognition models.
neurips-2021-dynamic-normalization-and-r.tldr: DNR improves video action recognition by adapting normalization through information shared across frames and network layers.

paragraphs: Many machine learning tasks require sampling from a distribution specified only through an unnormalized probability or energy function. Markov chain Monte Carlo methods are widely used, but convergence can be slow. Learning an auxiliary neural model can accelerate sampling at an additional training cost. This paper develops a different approach based on deterministic Hamiltonian dynamics.

The proposed Energy Sampling Hamiltonian dynamics use non-Newtonian momentum in an extended state space and require no stochastic step. Under an ergodicity assumption, the dynamics sample the target distribution exactly. The authors also interpret the method as a normalizing flow that samples a specified energy model without training. The assumption is essential to the stated exact-sampling result.

Existing ordinary differential equation solvers can handle the dynamics, but the authors derive a specialized solver with substantially better performance. They report faster convergence than the MCMC competitors, enabling faster and more stable training of neural energy models. The contribution combines a conditional theoretical sampling result with a numerical method intended to make that result useful in practice.
neurips-2021-hamiltonian-dynamics-with-n.tldr: Energy Sampling Hamiltonian dynamics provide deterministic sampling that is exact under ergodicity and faster than the tested MCMC competitors.

paragraphs: Animal movement sequences contain information about how individuals influence one another. Granger causality provides a framework for studying such interactions from time series, but it can overlook assumptions about how animal behavior generates the observations. This paper argues that ignoring those structures can make causal interpretations misleading and proposes incorporating behavioral theory directly into the analysis.

The method augments incomplete, time-varying behavioral models with interpretable neural components. Its architecture separates navigation from motion, while theory-guided regularization supports reliable behavioral modeling. This combination is designed to learn interactions efficiently and express the signs of Granger-causal effects over time, indicating when another animal's influence is associated with approach or separation.

On synthetic datasets, the method performs better than the compared baselines. The authors also analyze trajectories from mice, flies, birds, and bats, reporting biological insights from those applications. The contribution is a way to connect learned interaction patterns with an explicit model of behavior. Its causal interpretation remains framed in terms of Granger causality, the framework used by the paper.
neurips-2021-learning-interaction-rules-.tldr: Combining behavioral models with neural components yields interpretable, time-varying Granger-causal interactions from animal trajectories.

paragraphs: A routing improvement model learns how to revise an existing route to obtain a better solution. This paper identifies a representation problem when using Transformers for that task: conventional positional encoding does not suit the cyclic structure of vehicle routes. It proposes the Dual-Aspect Collaborative Transformer, or DACT, to represent route information more appropriately.

DACT learns separate embeddings for node features and positional features. Keeping these aspects separate is intended to avoid noise and incompatible correlations introduced by combining them directly. A cyclic positional encoding represents the circularity and symmetry of route solutions. The authors train the model with Proximal Policy Optimization and introduce a curriculum learning strategy to improve sample efficiency.

The evaluation covers the traveling salesman problem and the capacitated vehicle routing problem. DACT outperforms the existing Transformer-based improvement models tested and generalizes substantially better across problem sizes on synthetic and benchmark instances. The results support matching the model's representation to the structure of routes, with the architecture and training strategy together providing a learned approach to iterative solution improvement.
neurips-2021-learning-to-iteratively-sol.tldr: DACT separates node and cyclic position representations to improve learned route refinement and generalization across problem sizes.

paragraphs: Structured latent variables let a learning model encode prior knowledge through discrete structures, but their discreteness complicates training. A common strategy represents a latent structure as the output of a perturbed algorithm and uses a differentiable substitute during optimization. This paper addresses the additional model restrictions and biased gradients that such substitutes can introduce.

The authors extend the Gumbel-Max trick to define distributions over structured domains and use score-function estimators for optimization. Their construction focuses on a family of recursive algorithms sharing a property called a stochastic invariant. That property enables reliable gradient estimates and control variates without imposing the additional constraints associated with the differentiable surrogates being avoided.

Experiments examine several structured latent-variable models and obtain results competitive with relaxation-based alternatives. The contribution is therefore an alternative training route that works directly with discrete structured choices through gradient estimation. The stated stochastic-invariant property identifies the algorithm family supporting the construction; the paper does not claim that the same method applies automatically to every combinatorial space.
neurips-2021-leveraging-recursive-gumbel.tldr: A recursive extension of Gumbel-Max trains structured latent-variable models through score-function estimates instead of differentiable surrogates.

paragraphs: This paper considers a model that encounters a sequence of changing data distributions and must keep adapting. New tasks arrive without labels, while knowledge from earlier tasks should remain useful. The setting combines unsupervised domain adaptation, which addresses distribution shifts, with continual learning, which addresses learning over time without losing earlier capabilities.

The authors identify a mismatch between the existing approaches they discuss and this combined setting. Domain adaptation methods require simultaneous access to source and target datasets, whereas continual learning methods handle labeled tasks. The proposed algorithm instead centers on consolidating the model's learned internal distribution so that accumulated knowledge can support generalization to newly arriving domains.

The method also uses experience replay to address catastrophic forgetting. These two components serve complementary purposes: the consolidated distribution supports adaptation, and replay helps retain knowledge of past tasks. The contribution is an algorithm organized around both requirements within one learning process. The abstract describes this mechanism and its intended benefits without reporting a numerical performance comparison or a formal guarantee of complete retention.
neurips-2021-lifelong-domain-adaptation-.tldr: The proposed algorithm combines internal-distribution consolidation and experience replay to adapt continually to unlabeled domains while retaining past knowledge.

paragraphs: Boundary value problems are ordinary differential equations whose solutions must satisfy specified boundary conditions. This paper develops a probabilistic solver that returns a distribution over possible solutions, making uncertainty part of the numerical result. Its goal is to make this approach practical at a quality and computational cost comparable to established non-probabilistic solvers.

The key modeling choice is a Gauss-Markov prior tailored specifically to boundary value problems. This structure allows the posterior distribution over the solution to be computed in linear time. The method also incorporates uncertainty quantification, mesh refinement, and hyperparameter adaptation, bringing several practical numerical decisions into the same probabilistic framework.

The authors demonstrate that these practical components improve the scheme's efficiency. The resulting solver combines competitive numerical quality and cost with uncertainty information and native compatibility with other statistical modeling components. This matters when a differential-equation solution is one part of a larger statistical workflow: the solver represents its output probabilistically, rather than providing only a single numerical approximation for subsequent analysis.
neurips-2021-linear-time-probabilistic-s.tldr: A tailored Gauss-Markov model enables linear-time probabilistic boundary value solving with uncertainty estimates and practical adaptive features.

paragraphs: Tensor networks can represent very high-dimensional objects compactly, making them attractive for learning models in enormous feature spaces. This paper asks how expressive such models are from a statistical learning perspective. It derives upper and lower bounds on VC dimension and pseudo-dimension, capacity measures relevant to classification and real-valued prediction.

The upper bounds cover linear models parameterized by arbitrary tensor network structures. Lower bounds for CP, Tensor Train, Tensor Ring, and Tucker decompositions establish the tightness of the general upper bound. Together, these results connect the structured representation of a model with how rich a collection of predictions it can express.

The authors use the capacity bounds to derive a generalization bound for classifiers based on low-rank matrices and common tensor decompositions. They also obtain a VC-dimension bound for the matrix product state classifier as a function of bond dimension, or tensor train rank, resolving a stated open problem. The contribution provides theoretical control over model capacity rather than an empirical comparison of predictive performance.
neurips-2021-lower-and-upper-bounds-on-t.tldr: Capacity bounds for tensor network models yield generalization guarantees and resolve an open question about matrix product state classifiers.

paragraphs: Neural network reliability requirements often involve uncertainty in the network or its inputs. This paper formulates probabilistic specifications that cover both cases, including Bayesian networks, dropout-based networks, and input distributions arising from noise or perturbations. The aim is to formally verify desired behavior when uncertainty is part of the system being evaluated.

The verification method generalizes Lagrangian duality by replacing ordinary multipliers with functions of intermediate layer activations. The authors prove that an optimal choice of these functional multipliers gives sound and complete verification. They then restrict the multiplier forms to obtain tractable algorithms. Exactness is therefore a result about the optimal construction, not an unconditional claim about every practical implementation.

Experiments certify adversarial robustness and robust detection of out-of-distribution inputs. The reported guarantees are stronger than prior ones: for example, certified AUC for one dropout network's robust detection task increases from 0% to 29%, while a Bayesian network's robust accuracy guarantee increases from 60.2% to 74.6%. These are improvements in what can be certified, including a lower bound on AUC, rather than claims of corresponding changes in ordinary predictive performance.
neurips-2021-make-sure-you-re-unsure-a-f.tldr: Functional multipliers extend neural network verification to probabilistic requirements and produce stronger practical robustness certificates.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning several related causal graphs together. The graphs describe Gaussian linear structural equation models and are assumed to share a consistent causal ordering, with a sparse union of their edge supports. Those assumptions provide a basis for sharing information across tasks while allowing their graph structures to differ.

The authors propose a joint maximum likelihood estimator with an l1/l2 regularizer. They prove that joint estimation can require fewer samples to recover the causal ordering than learning each graph separately. They also show that a graph that is not identifiable on its own can become recoverable when estimated together with some identifiable graphs under the studied setting.

The analysis additionally establishes consistency for recovering the union of graph supports. To make the estimator implementable, the authors formulate a continuous optimization problem with the same optimizer and develop an iterative algorithm to approximate it efficiently. Experiments support the theory and effectiveness of joint estimation. The result explains how shared ordering and structural sparsity can turn related tasks into useful evidence for causal discovery.
neurips-2021-multi-task-learning-of-orde.tldr: Jointly learning related Gaussian causal graphs can improve sample complexity and recover otherwise non-identifiable graphs under shared-order and sparsity assumptions.

paragraphs: Factored Markov decision processes describe decision problems through a structured set of interacting components. This paper studies regret minimization in the non-episodic setting, where learning proceeds without division into separate episodes. It addresses an assumption made by the existing algorithms discussed in the abstract: that the learner already knows the process's factored structure.

The proposed algorithm learns that structure while also minimizing regret. It combines optimism in the face of uncertainty with a statistical method for structure learning. Its implementation is efficient given access to a planning oracle for factored decision processes. This qualification separates the efficiency of the learning procedure from the availability of the planner it calls.

The authors also provide a variant that remains efficient when the oracle supports only non-factored actions, matching a restriction of almost all existing approximate planners. Finally, they derive a new lower bound for the case where structure is known, closing a stated gap with an existing regret bound. The paper thus addresses both learning unknown dependencies and understanding limits in the known-structure setting.
neurips-2021-oracle-efficient-regret-min.tldr: An optimistic algorithm learns unknown factored MDP structure while minimizing regret, with efficiency conditional on access to a planning oracle.

paragraphs: Domain generalization asks whether a model trained on source domains will work on a different target domain. Many methods seek invariant features, hoping that a strong source classifier will also perform well elsewhere. This paper focuses on the next question: how to quantify whether learned features actually support that transfer.

The authors formally define a computable notion of transferability and explain its relationship to domain discrepancy measures such as total variation and Wasserstein distance. They prove that transferability can be estimated with enough samples and derive an upper bound on target error using it. This connects a measurable feature property with a theoretical statement about performance after transfer.

Empirical evaluation finds that many existing domain generalization algorithms do not learn particularly transferable features under the proposed measure, although some do. Guided by this finding, the authors introduce an algorithm designed to learn transferable features. Across RotatedMNIST, PACS, Office-Home, and WILDS-FMoW, it consistently improves over many state-of-the-art methods tested. The contribution combines a diagnostic definition, an error bound, and a learning approach informed by both.
neurips-2021-quantifying-and-improving-t.tldr: A formal measure of feature transferability supports target-error bounds and an algorithm that improves performance across several domain generalization benchmarks.

paragraphs: Dropout regularizes neural network training by introducing randomness, but that randomness also creates inconsistency between training and inference. R-Drop addresses this by encouraging different dropout-generated versions of the same model to make similar probabilistic predictions. The method adds a consistency objective to training rather than introducing a new network architecture.

For each training example, R-Drop samples two submodels through dropout and compares their output distributions. It minimizes KL divergence in both directions between those distributions, encouraging agreement despite the different dropout samples. The paper's theoretical analysis shows that this strategy reduces the training–inference inconsistency motivating the method.

Experiments cover five tasks and eighteen datasets, spanning language and image applications, and report effectiveness throughout that evaluation. The authors find substantial gains when fine-tuning large pretrained models. They also report state-of-the-art translation results with a vanilla Transformer, including 30.91 BLEU for WMT14 English-to-German and 43.95 for English-to-French. The findings show broad empirical value for a simple distribution-matching regularizer across the settings tested.
neurips-2021-r-drop-regularized-dropout-.tldr: R-Drop improves training by making two dropout-generated predictions for each example agree through bidirectional KL regularization.

paragraphs: Visual question answering and referring expression recognition require connecting language with objects and relationships in an image. This paper identifies a weakness in earlier neural module networks: their modules do not adequately link visual information with the relevant surrounding text. That can make unfamiliar combinations of familiar concepts difficult to understand.

The proposed language-guided adaptive convolution layer modifies convolution filters using a spatially varying kernel guided by language. This lets each neural module adapt its attention jointly across visual and textual inputs when identifying potential objects of interest. The mechanism aims to make the visual computation sensitive to the contextual meaning of the expression being processed.

Experiments on visual question answering and referring expression recognition demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. The authors also introduce C3-Ref+, an out-of-distribution test split for referring expressions that evaluates adversarial perturbations and unseen combinations of known concepts. Results on this split provide further evidence of generalization. The contribution couples a concrete language-conditioned computation with an evaluation aimed directly at the compositional failures motivating the design.
neurips-2021-robust-visual-reasoning-via.tldr: Language-guided adaptive convolutions improve neural module networks' visual reasoning and generalization to tested perturbations and new concept combinations.

paragraphs: This paper studies a learner trying to identify the best option when each option's value depends linearly on an unknown parameter. Potential measurements arrive independently from the same distribution. The learner can pay for a noisy measurement or skip it and wait, creating a trade-off between acquiring fewer labels and reaching a decision sooner.

The goal is to identify the best option with a specified high probability. The authors characterize the relationship between the number of measurements taken and the stopping time. They provide an algorithm that nearly achieves the smallest label requirement for a chosen stopping-time target, making the time-versus-information trade-off explicit.

The analysis also shows that the optimal measurement decision has a simple geometric description based on whether an arriving point lies inside an ellipse. This connects a sequential statistical decision with a concrete rule for selecting observations. The framework additionally covers binary classification and improves on previous work in that setting. Its guarantees concern the stated linear measurement model and independently arriving stream.
neurips-2021-selective-sampling-for-onli.tldr: The paper characterizes how selective measurement trades label cost against decision time and gives a nearly optimal best-option identification algorithm.

paragraphs: Class-incremental semantic segmentation requires learning to label new object classes while preserving earlier segmentation knowledge. The paper highlights two challenges that contribute to forgetting: the changing meaning of the background class and the need to handle multiple labels. Its proposed SSUL-M method combines techniques aimed specifically at these segmentation issues.

First, the method represents an unknown class within the background, helping prepare for categories that will be learned later. Second, it freezes the backbone and previous classifiers while using binary cross-entropy and pseudo-labeling to support retention. Third, it keeps a tiny memory of example data, which the authors use to improve both learning new classes and preserving old ones.

The authors report significantly better performance than recent state-of-the-art baselines on standard benchmarks. Extensive ablation analyses examine the contributions of the method's components. The approach matters because it treats adaptation and retention as related design requirements and accounts for the special role of background in segmentation. The results support the combined method on the evaluated datasets rather than implying that forgetting has been eliminated universally.
neurips-2021-ssul-semantic-segmentation-.tldr: SSUL-M combines an unknown background class, frozen earlier components, and a small exemplar memory to improve incremental semantic segmentation.

paragraphs: A language model may learn a task from a few examples while still relying on many additional examples to choose prompts or hyperparameters. This paper examines few-shot learning when those held-out examples are unavailable. It calls this true few-shot learning and makes model selection part of the difficulty being measured.

The authors test cross-validation and minimum description length as ways to choose prompts and hyperparameters from scarce data. On average, both perform only slightly better than random selection and substantially worse than selection using held-out examples. They also frequently select models that perform considerably worse than randomly chosen alternatives, showing that the average advantage can conceal unreliable choices.

Similar results persist when selection accounts for uncertainty about model performance and when the authors vary computation and the number of examples used. The findings suggest that earlier work substantially overestimated true few-shot ability by benefiting from additional selection data. The central implication is that learning from a few examples and reliably choosing how to learn from them are both necessary parts of evaluating this setting.
neurips-2021-true-few-shot-learning-with.tldr: Without held-out selection examples, tested prompt and hyperparameter selection methods barely beat random choice on average, challenging earlier few-shot evaluations.

paragraphs: Combining several data modalities often improves empirical performance, but an intuitive appeal to additional information does not by itself explain when learning should improve. This paper develops a theoretical account within a common fusion framework: features from different modalities enter a shared latent representation, which is then mapped to the task output.

Within the framework studied, the authors prove that learning with multiple modalities achieves lower population risk than learning with only a subset. The explanation centers on the quality of the latent representation: the additional modalities allow it to be estimated more accurately. This links the benefit of fusion to representation learning and performance on the underlying data population.

The paper combines its analysis with experimental results to support the formal account. Its contribution is a generalization-based explanation for qualitative behavior observed in multimodal applications. The guarantee belongs to the analyzed fusion setting; it should not be read as saying that adding any modality to any system must improve predictions. The result clarifies how better shared representations can support a multimodal advantage.
neurips-2021-what-makes-multi-modal-lear.tldr: Within a shared-latent-space fusion framework, the paper proves a multimodal population-risk advantage through more accurate latent representations.
